text.tspan: One call, and the only slow line in the whole notebook: relearning it took about
is a list of five strings: the
. The sentences are included on purpose, so every word this model will ever see is guaranteed
to end up as a single token rather than fragments.
turns "The" and "the" into the same word, and
cuts at spaces — which means punctuation stays stuck to its word, so "sofa." and "sofa" would count as
different words. Neither matters for these sentences, but both matter a lot for real text; production tokenizers handle
capitals and punctuation far more carefully.
of those, from the word list
Each word is stored as a LIST of characters, not a string, because the
loop will keep replacing these lists with
shorter, merged versions. Notice that every occurrence is stored separately: "the" appears thousands of times in the
, so it becomes thousands of separate entries. That repetition is what gives the pair counts in
meaning — a pair found in many words gets a big count.
The starting point of BPE: a word becomes a list of single characters, and every
list shorter. Because the starting alphabet is just the characters that actually occur, any word made of those
characters can be written down — the worst case is simply a word that needs many pieces. That is why the
This loop is where all the learning happens. Each pass finds the single most common pair of neighbouring
and glues that pair together everywhere at once. It is greedy (it always takes the top pair), global
(it looks at every word at once) and deterministic: running it twice on the same
same order. The order matters, because
Every pass starts by counting every pair of neighbours from scratch, across every word — which is why training
takes minutes rather than seconds. Pairs are only counted INSIDE a word: the loop stops one
end, so a pair never crosses a space and "the dog" can never become a single token. The table shows the most
common pairs on the very first pass.
distinct adjacent pairs on the first pass, most frequent first

Every word in these sentences ends up as a single token, so this page never shows BPE doing the job it exists for: handling a word it has never seen. Here is that case, run through the same

text.tspan: An unknown word costs positions, not meaning
— "qu" + "ok" + "ka". Nothing later on notices or complains: the sentence is simply
longer than it would be for a known word. Each
piece gets its own embedding, its own position and its own row in the attention tables, and the model has to work out from context that they belong together. That is
the whole case for subword tokenization — the
stays a fixed size, no input is ever impossible to represent, and a rare word costs a few extra positions
returns bare characters, so the piece "the" carries
no record of whether it was a whole word or the start of "theory".
hides this by putting a space between every token — so a word split into
separate fragments with spaces between them, and the round trip does not give back the original text. Real tokenizers mark word boundaries
puts the space inside the token, the original BPE adds "</w>") precisely so decoding can be exact.
sequence A — "the dog sat on the floor" (padded by
sequence B — "the cat is sleeping on the sofa" (no padding — it sets the width)
